applies trigonometry to solve problems involving geometric shapes
Content
Trigonometry with acute angles
Use Pythagoras’ theorem to find the exact sine, cosine and tangent ratios for angles of 30° , 45° and 60°
Apply trigonometry to solve problems involving right-angled triangles in two dimensions, true and compass bearings, and angles of elevation and depression
Trigonometry with angles of any magnitude
Represent angles of any magnitude using rays from the origin in the Cartesian plane and describe how one ray represents infinitely many angles
Develop the definitions cos⁡θ=(x)/(r) , sin⁡θ=(y)/(r) and tan⁡θ=(y)/(x) , where (x,y) is a point on the circle of radius r , centred at the origin, and θ is the angle between the positive x -axis and the radius drawn to this point
Use the definitions cos⁡θ=(x)/(r) , sin⁡θ=(y)/(r) and tan⁡θ=(y)/(x) to evaluate sin⁡θ , cos⁡θ and tan⁡θ where θ is a multiple of 90° , and identify the values of θ for which these ratios are undefined
Extend and apply the definitions cos⁡θ=(x)/(r) , sin⁡θ=(y)/(r) and tan⁡θ=(y)/(x) for angles of any magnitude
Identify the related angle of an angle of any magnitude, excluding multiples of 90° , as the acute angle between the ray and the x -axis and obtain the values of the trigonometric functions of an angle of any magnitude from the trigonometric functions of the related angle
Develop and use the trigonometric ratios for angles that can be written in the form θ=180°±A , and θ=360°-A , where 0°<A<90°
Find the exact value of sin⁡(-120°) and tan⁡585° .
Establish and use the results cos⁡(-θ)=cos⁡θ , sin⁡(-θ)=-sin⁡θ and tan⁡(-θ)=-tan⁡θ
Examine the proof of the sine rule (a)/(sin⁡A)=(b)/(sin⁡B )=(c)/(sin⁡C) , cosine rule (c)^(2)=(a)^(2)+(b)^(2)-2abcos⁡C and the area of a triangle formula A=(1)/(2)absin⁡C for a given triangle ABC
Use graphing applications or geometric construction to examine the ambiguous case of the sine rule, in which there are two possible solutions for an angle, and the condition for it to arise
Image long description: A triangle ABC' with sides b and c contains a smaller triangle with 2 sides b . The internal side b intersects line BC' at point C . An arc connects points C and C' , demonstrating that the movement of point C can adjust the angle ACB so it is either obtuse or acute.
Apply the sine rule, cosine rule and formula for the area of a triangle to solve problems where angles are measured in degrees, or degrees and minutes
Radians
Recognise that both ratios (arc length)/(circumference) and (area of sector)/(area of circle) are equal to (θ)/(one revolution) where θ is the angle at the centre of a circle subtended by the arc
Define the angle size of θ in radian measure as the ratio (arc length)/(radius of a circle)
Explain why 360°=2π radians and 1 radian=(180)/(π) degrees
Convert between degrees and radians and find the exact sine, cosine and tangent ratios for integer multiples of (π)/(6) and (π)/(4)
Graph y=sin x , y=cos x and y=tan x over domains given in degrees or radians, showing intercepts with the x -axis and y -axis and any asymptotes, determine their domains and ranges, and period and amplitude where appropriate, and whether each is even or odd or neither
Establish and use the formula l=rθ for the length l of arc subtending an angle θ in radians at the centre of a circle of radius r
Prove and use the formula A=(1)/(2)(r)^(2)θ for the area of a sector with angle θ in radians at the centre of a circle of radius r
Solve problems involving arc lengths and areas of major and minor sectors and segments

content.value:
• Some students may need to review Pythagoras’ theorem and its proof in preparation for applying the theorem in a wider variety of situations.
  • Some students may benefit from a review of the sine, cosine and tangent ratios for angles in right-angled triangles. They may need to revisit the concept of similarity and use it to explain the constancy of trigonometric ratios for triangles of the same shape but different sizes.
  • Students could use aids such as CAST or mnemonics such as All Stations To Central (ASTC) related to which quadrants of the unit circle contain positive results for sin⁡θ, cos⁡θ and tan⁡θ.
  • Proofs of the sine rule, cosine rule and area rule should be examined by students. Students are not expected to reproduce these proofs.
  • The sine rule may be expressed as: ‘in a given triangle ABC, the ratio of a side to the sine of the opposite angle is a constant’.
  • After the cosine rule is introduced, students could compare it with Pythagoras’ theorem and conclude that Pythagoras’ theorem is a special case of the cosine rule.
  • When working with radians, ‘sin⁡3’ means the sine of an angle whose circular measure is 3, and this may be read as ‘sin⁡3 radians’ to distinguish it from sin⁡3°, the sine of an angle of 3 degrees.

Purpose

The study of trigonometric functions involves using periodic functions in geometric, algebraic, numerical and graphical representations and is important in developing students’ understanding of periodic behaviour. A knowledge of trigonometric functions enables the solving of practical problems involving triangles or periodic graphs. Using the periodicity of trigonometric functions, mathematical models have been developed that describe the behaviour of many naturally occurring periodic phenomena, such as vibrations or waves, as well as oscillatory behaviour found in pendulums, electric currents and radio signals.

Year 11: Trigonometric identities and equations
Outcomes
MAO-WM-01:
develops understanding and fluency in mathematics through exploring and connecting mathematical concepts, choosing and applying mathematical techniques to solve problems, and communicating their thinking and reasoning coherently and clearly
MAV-11-05:
uses periodic functions to solve trigonometric equations and prove trigonometric identities
Content
Define the trigonometric functions sec⁡θ , cosecθ and cot⁡θ for acute angles θ using ratios of sides in a right-angled triangle
Find the exact secant, cosecant and cotangent ratios for angles of 30° , 45° and 60°
Justify the values of sec⁡θ , cosecθ and cot⁡θ at 0° and 90° by examining the ratios of sides in a right-angled triangle as θ tends to 0° and 90°
Develop the definitions sec⁡θ=(r)/(x) , cosecθ=(r)/(y) and cot⁡θ=(x)/(y) using a circle of radius r centred at the origin
Establish the reciprocal ratios sec⁡A=(1)/(cos⁡A) , cosec⁡A=(1)/(sin⁡A) , and cot⁡A=(1)/(tan⁡A) , identifying the angles to be excluded in each identity
Determine the exact value of the secant, cosecant and cotangent ratios for angles that are integer multiples of (π)/(6) and (π)/(4) , if they exist
Establish the identities tan⁡θ=(sin⁡θ)/(cos⁡θ) and cot⁡θ=(cos⁡θ)/(sin⁡θ) , identifying the angles to be excluded in each identity
Prove the complementary angle identities sin⁡(90°-θ)=cos⁡θ , cos⁡(90°-θ)=sin⁡θ , tan⁡(90°-θ)=cot⁡θ , cot⁡(90°-θ)=tan⁡θ , sec⁡(90°-θ)=cosec⁡θ and cosec⁡(90°-θ)=sec⁡θ identifying the angles to be excluded in each identity
Evaluate trigonometric expressions using angles of any magnitude and complementary angle identities
Given cot α=-(15)/(8) , and that (π)/(2)<α<π , find the values of cosec α and cos⁡α .
Solve equations involving trigonometric ratios of angles, specified in degrees or radians, on a restricted domain
Solve sqrt(3)sin⁡x=cos⁡x for 0°≤x≤360° and 2cos⁡2x=0 for -π≤x≤π .
Prove the Pythagorean identity (cos)^(2)⁡x+(sin)^(2)⁡x=1 , and the identities 1+(tan)^(2)⁡x=(sec)^(2)⁡x and 1+(cot)^(2)⁡x=(cosec)^(2)⁡x
Apply trigonometric identities to solve problems, simplify expressions and prove further trigonometric identities using substitution and/or reduction to sin⁡x and cos⁡x
Prove that (sec)^(2)⁡x+sec⁡xtan⁡x=(1+sin⁡x)/((cos)^(2)⁡x) and hence prove that (sec)^(2)⁡x+sec⁡xtan⁡x=(1)/(1-sin⁡x) .
Solve problems involving trigonometric equations, including those that reduce to quadratic equations, on a restricted domain
Express 5(cot)^(2)⁡x-2cosec⁡x+2 in terms of cosec⁡x and hence solve the equation 5(cot)^(2)⁡x-2cosec⁡x+2=0 for 0≤x<2π .

content.name: 📜 Content
content.value:
Purpose

The study of trigonometric functions involves using periodic functions in geometric, algebraic, numerical and graphical representations. Knowledge of trigonometric functions enables the solving of practical problems involving triangles or periodic graphs, such as waves and signals.

The study of trigonometric functions is important in developing students’ understanding of periodic behaviour. Using the periodicity of trigonometric functions, mathematical models have been developed that describe the behaviour of many naturally occurring periodic phenomena, such as vibrations or waves, as well as oscillatory behaviour found in pendulums, electric currents and radio signals.

Key terms

  • complementary angle
  • cosecant ratio
  • cosine ratio
  • cotangent ratio
  • radian
  • secant ratio
  • sine ratio
  • tangent ratio

Related Stage 5 Path content

  • Functions and other graphs
  • Trigonometry C
  • Trigonometry D

Sequencing advice

The content in the focus area Trigonometric identities and equations builds on content in:

  • Mathematics Advanced Year 11 Working with functions
  • Mathematics Advanced Year 11 Trigonometry and measure of angles.

Making connections

ConnectionsCourse/Stage/Focus area/Post-school paths
Solving trigonometric equations may involve equations reducible to quadratic equations.Mathematics Stage 5 Equations C
Proving trigonometric identities requires the process of proof.Mathematics Stage 5 Properties of geometrical figures C
The definition of secant, cosecant and cotangent ratios can be developed using a circle centred at the origin.Mathematics Advanced Year 11 Working with functions
Secant, cosecant and cotangent functions can be used in differentiation.

The secant function is used in integration.

Mathematics Advanced Year 12

  • Differential calculus
  • Integral calculus
Secant, cosecant and cotangent functions can be used in solving three-dimensional geometry problems, proving trigonometric identities and solving trigonometric equations.

Mathematics Extension 1 Year 11 Further trigonometry


Graphs of secant, cosecant and cotangent functions can be considered as graphs of reciprocal functions.Mathematics Extension 1 Year 11 Further work with functions
Complementary identities are used in proving identities involving inverse trigonometric functions and Pythagorean identities are used in proving the double angle identities.

Mathematics Extension 1 Year 12

  • Inverse trigonometric functions
  • Further calculus skills
Trigonometric equations and identities are used when modelling quantities that vary in a cyclical way such as tides, seasons, demand for resources and alternating current.Mathematics Advanced Year 12 Further graph transformations and modelling

Mathematics Extension 1 Year 11 Further trigonometry

Mathematics Extension 2 Year 12 Applications of calculus to mechanics
Proof by mathematical induction can be used to prove trigonometric identities.Mathematics Extension 2 Year 12 The nature of proof

Considerations

Year 11: Trigonometric identities and equations

Outcomes

MAO-WM-01:

develops understanding and fluency in mathematics through exploring and connecting mathematical concepts, choosing and applying mathematical techniques to solve problems, and communicating their thinking and reasoning coherently and clearly

MAV-11-05:

uses periodic functions to solve trigonometric equations and prove trigonometric identities

Content


  • Define the trigonometric functions sec⁡θ, cosecθ and cot⁡θ for acute angles θ using ratios of sides in a right-angled triangle



  • Find the exact secant, cosecant and cotangent ratios for angles of 30°, 45° and 60°



  • Justify the values of sec⁡θ, cosecθ and cot⁡θ at 0° and 90° by examining the ratios of sides in a right-angled triangle as θ tends to 0° and 90°



  • Develop the definitions sec⁡θ=rx, cosecθ=ry and cot⁡θ=xy using a circle of radius r centred at the origin



  • Establish the reciprocal ratios sec⁡A=1cos⁡A, cosec⁡A=1sin⁡A, and cot⁡A=1tan⁡A, identifying the angles to be excluded in each identity



  • Determine the exact value of the secant, cosecant and cotangent ratios for angles that are integer multiples of π6 and π4, if they exist



  • Establish the identities tan⁡θ=sin⁡θcos⁡θ and cot⁡θ=cos⁡θsin⁡θ, identifying the angles to be excluded in each identity



  • Prove the complementary angle identities sin⁡(90°-θ)=cos⁡θ, cos⁡(90°-θ)=sin⁡θ, tan⁡(90°-θ)=cot⁡θ, cot⁡(90°-θ)=tan⁡θ, sec⁡(90°-θ)=cosec⁡θ and cosec⁡(90°-θ)=sec⁡θ identifying the angles to be excluded in each identity



  • Evaluate trigonometric expressions using angles of any magnitude and complementary angle identities


    Given cot α=-158, and that π2<α<π, find the values of cosec α and cos⁡α.

  • Solve equations involving trigonometric ratios of angles, specified in degrees or radians, on a restricted domain


    Solve 3sin⁡x=cos⁡x for 0°≤x≤360° and 2cos⁡2x=0 for -π≤x≤π.

  • Prove the Pythagorean identity cos2⁡x+sin2⁡x=1, and the identities 1+tan2⁡x=sec2⁡x and 1+cot2⁡x=cosec2⁡x



  • Apply trigonometric identities to solve problems, simplify expressions and prove further trigonometric identities using substitution and/or reduction to sin⁡x and cos⁡x


    Prove that sec2⁡x+sec⁡xtan⁡x=1+sin⁡xcos2⁡x and hence prove that sec2⁡x+sec⁡xtan⁡x=11-sin⁡x.

  • Solve problems involving trigonometric equations, including those that reduce to quadratic equations, on a restricted domain


    Express 5cot2⁡x-2cosec⁡x+2 in terms of cosec⁡x and hence solve the equation 5cot2⁡x-2cosec⁡x+2=0 for 0≤x<2π.

Apply the chain rule: if  y is a differentiable function of u , and u is a differentiable function of x , then (dy)/(dx) = (dy)/(du)×(du)/(dx) or if h(x)=f(g(x)) for differentiable functions f(x) and g(x) then h'(x)=f'(g(x))g'(x)

content.name: 📜 Content
content.value:
Connections

Course/Stage/Focus area/Post-school paths

Negative values have significance for displacement and velocity. They indicate direction from the original position.

Mathematics Stage 4 Computation with integers

Determining the gradient between points is important for finding the gradient of a secant.

Mathematics Advanced Year 11 Working with functions

Finding the tangent or normal to a curve involves the use of the point–gradient form of a straight line.

Mathematics Advanced Year 11 Working with functions

Function notation is important when considering derivatives.

Mathematics Stage 5 Functions and other graphs

Mathematics Advanced Year 11 Working with functions

The nature of stationary points can be determined by considering the second derivative.

Mathematics Advanced Year 12 Applications of calculus

Finding the distance travelled by a particle involves considering the nature of stationary points.

Mathematics Advanced Year 12 Applications of calculus

The probability density function can be determined by finding the derivative of the cumulative distribution function.

Mathematics Advanced Year 12 Random variables

The derivative can be used to determine the multiplicity of roots of polynomials.

Mathematics Extension 1 Year 11 Polynomials

The uniqueness of Euler’s number, e, can be shown using differentiation.

Mathematics Advanced Year 11 Exponential and logarithmic functions

Derivatives can be used to find the velocity, acceleration and momentum of a moving body.

Change in concentration of an element involved in a chemical reaction can be predicted using differentiation.

Derivatives can be used to predict the results of different investment possibilities and to find the rate of blood flow, the rate of dissolution of drugs into the bloodstream, shrinkage of the number of cells in a cancerous tumour and the growth of bacteria.

Applications of calculus are prevalent in the field of engineering.

Real-world applications

Purpose

In differential calculus, the idea of ‘gradient as a rate of change’ is used to find the rates of change of functions with non-constant rates of change. These functions are represented geometrically by curves. The process of finding these rates of change is known as differentiation. This process is of fundamental importance in mathematics and has applications in all quantitative fields of study, including physics, chemistry, medicine, engineering, computing, statistics, business, finance and economics.

content.value:
• For differentiation by first principles Δx is sometimes used in place of h, and the alternate definition of differentiation by first principles is sometimes used: f'c=limx→c⁡fx-fcx-c.
  • The terms ‘maximum magnitude of velocity’ or ‘maximum speed’ should be used when discussing velocity rather than ambiguous language such as ‘maximum velocity’.
  • Note that the limit f'x=limh→0fx+h-fxh may fail to exist even for a continuous curve: the curve may have a vertical tangent (infinite slope) as in fx=x13 at x=0, or a sharp bend, as in y=|x| at x=0.
  • Some students may benefit from extension that involves finding the derivative of fx=x3, fx=x and fx=1x by first principles but this is not essential content.
  • Some students may benefit from extension that involves consideration of concepts such as:
    • whether a function is increasing or decreasing on an interval: a function f(x) is said to be increasing on an interval if for all a≤b in the interval, fa≤f(b), and decreasing on an interval if for all a≤b in the interval, fa≥f(b).
    • whether a function is strictly increasing if f'x>0 over an interval or strictly decreasing if f'x<0  on an interval.
  • Some students may benefit from extension that involves deriving the following results, though this is not essential content: if u and v are differentiable functions of x, then:
    if y=ku, y'=ku' where k is a constant
    if y=u±v, y'=u'±v'
    if y=fu, y'=f'uu' (for any differentiable function f)
    if y=uv, y'=uv'+u'v
    if y=uv, y'=vu'-uv'v2, (v≠0).

Year 11: Introduction to differentiation

Outcomes

MAO-WM-01:

develops understanding and fluency in mathematics through exploring and connecting mathematical concepts, choosing and applying mathematical techniques to solve problems, and communicating their thinking and reasoning coherently and clearly

MAV-11-06:

interprets the meaning of the derivative and determines the derivative of functions to solve problems

Content

Estimating change


  • Define the average rate of change of y with respect to x for a function y=fx over the domain [a,b] as Δ y Δ x = change in  y change in  x , that is Δ y Δ x = f b - f ( a ) b - a , and recognise fb-f(a)b-a as the gradient of the secant through a,fa and b,fb on the graph of y=f(x)



  • Recognise speed as a rate of change of distance with respect to time



  • Use the definition for average rate of change to determine the average speed of an object from a given distance–time graph



  • Describe the difference between the average speed of an object and its instantaneous speed



  • Determine that the instantaneous speed of an object at time t can be approximated by the average speed between its position at time t and its position some time later, and explain how this approximation can be improved



  • Relate the instantaneous speed of an object to the gradient of the tangent at that point on its distance–time graph



  • Estimate the instantaneous speed of an object from its distance–time graph



  • Recognise when modelling with a linear function that its gradient is the rate of change and determine the rate of change for linear functions in practical situations



  • Recognise when modelling with a non-linear function that the rate of change is not constant and is represented by the gradient of the tangent to the curve at each point on the curve



  • Estimate the instantaneous rate of change of a non-linear function at a given point from a given graph of a practical situation


    The graph shows the displacement of a particle that is moving in a horizontal line. Estimate the velocity of the particle as it passes through the origin.

    Image long description: A graph of a distance–time function with displacement in metres on the y-axis and time in minutes on the x-axis. It depicts a distance-time function that is in the shape of a concave down parabola with a distance intercept of 5 metres and time intercept of 5 minutes. The vertex of the parabola is at the point (2, 9).

The derivative


  • Examine the gradient of a curve at a point on the curve using graphing applications


    Use a graphing application to magnify the graph of y=x2 at x=1. Discuss the ‘straightness’ of the graph when magnified.

  • Approximate the gradient of a curve f(x)=xn at a point Pc,fc by considering the gradient of the secant through P and Qc+h,fc+h as the magnitude of h approaches zero, using graphing applications or a spreadsheet


    Use a spreadsheet or graphing application to examine the gradient of f(x)=xn, n=2 and 3 at P(c,fc) for various values of c by considering the value of fc+h-f(c)h as h steadily decreases.

  • Infer that nxn-1 is the gradient of fx=xn and verify the result using graphing applications


    Use a graphing application to find an approximation for the gradient of f(x)=xn by considering the graph of y=fx+0.001-f(x)h for n=2 and 3. Summarise the results for the gradients of y=1, y=x, y=x2 and y=x3 and generalise the result for y=xn.

    Use a graphing application to verify the result for positive, negative and fractional values of n.

  • Define f'(x), for any function f(x) and any value x, to be the gradient of the tangent to the curve y=f(x) at the point Px,fx if the tangent exists and is not vertical



  • Refer to f'(x) as the derivative of f(x) or the gradient, or derived, function of f(x)



  • Define differentiation as the process of finding the derivative of a function



  • Find derivatives of constant and linear functions



  • Define the derivative of the function fx from first principles, as the limiting value of the gradient of the secant fx+h-fxh as h approaches zero, when this limiting value exists, and use the notation f'x=limh→0fx+h-fxh



  • Use first principles to find the derivative of quadratic functions


    Use differentiation by first principles to verify that if y=3x2-x, then y'=6x-1.

Calculations with the derivative


  • Use the notation dydx and y' for the derivative of y when y is a function of x



  • Use the notation ddxfx and f'(x) for the derivative of a function fx



  • Use the formula ddx(xn)=nxn-1 for all real values of n


    Find the derivative of fx=x7, ft=t and gx=1x3.

  • Apply the fact that the derivative of a sum is the sum of the derivatives: ddxfx+gx=f'x+g'(x), and the derivative of a multiple of a function is the multiple of its derivative: ddx(k⋅fx)=k⋅f'(x)



  • Use the rules for differentiation to find equations of tangents and normals to a curve at points on the curve



  • Find points on a curve where the tangent or normal has a given gradient



  • Examine and use the relationship between the angle of inclination of a line or tangent to a curve, θ, with the positive x-axis, and the gradient, m, of that line or tangent, and establish that tan⁡θ=m



  • Apply the product rule: if y=uv, where u and v are both differentiable functions of x, then dydx=udvdx+vdudx or if h(x)=f(x)g(x) for differentiable functions f(x) and g(x) then h'x=fxg'x+f'xg(x) 



  • Apply the quotient rule: if y=uv, where u and v are both differentiable functions of x, then dydx=vdudx-udvdxv2 or if hx=fxgx then h'x=gxf'x-fxg'x[gx]2



  • Apply the chain rule: if y is a differentiable function of u, and u is a differentiable function of x, then dydx = dydu×dudx or if hx=fgx for differentiable functions f(x) and g(x) then h'x=f'gxg'x



  • Identify and apply the product, quotient or chain rule, or a combination of the rules, as appropriate to differentiate a given function



Graphical applications of the derivative


  • Interpret fx as increasing at x=c when f'c>0 and decreasing at x=c when f'c<0



  • Describe the behaviour of a function at a point as stationary when the tangent at the point is parallel to the x-axis, and recognise that fx is stationary at x=c when f'c=0



  • Graph y=f'(x) for a given graph of a function y=f(x)



  • Numerically estimate the value of the derivative at a point on the graph of a power of x, with and without the use of digital tools



  • Identify stationary points on the graph of a cubic function, and the values of x for which the function is increasing and/or decreasing, by first calculating the derivative, and justify conclusions



The derivative as a rate of change


  • Interpret f'(c) as the instantaneous rate of change of the function f(x) at x=c



  • Define and distinguish between displacement and distance and between velocity and speed



  • Use graphs of functions and their derivatives, without the use of algebraic techniques, to describe and interpret physical phenomena



  • Use the notation dxdt or ẋ to represent the velocity of a particle with displacement x from a point as a function of time t



  • Solve problems by determining the velocity of a particle moving in a straight line, given its displacement from a point as a function of time

Outcomes
MAO-WM-01:
develops understanding and fluency in mathematics through exploring and connecting mathematical concepts, choosing and applying mathematical techniques to solve problems, and communicating their thinking and reasoning coherently and clearly
MAV-11-07:
applies exponential and logarithmic laws to simplify expressions, solve equations and prove results
MAV-11-08:
analyses graphs of exponential and logarithmic functions
Content
Exponential functions
Graph the exponential functions  y=k((a)^(x)) and y=k((a)^(-x)) for constants a and k where a>0 , a≠1 and k≠0 , and identify its asymptote, y -intercept, domain and range
Describe the behaviour of y=k((a)^(x)) and y=k((a)^(-x)) as x→∞ and x→-∞
For y=(2)^(x) , as x→-∞ , y→0 and as x→∞ , y→∞ .
Examine the gradient of the tangent to the curve y=(a)^(x) at its y -intercept for varying values of a , and verify using graphing applications that there is a unique number
e≈2.71828182845 ..., such that the gradient of the tangent to y=(e)^(x) at x=0 is 1, and call this number e Euler’s number
Examine the gradient function of y=(a)^(x) with graphing applications and identify that the gradient function is (d)/(dx)((a)^(x))=k(a)^(x) , for some constant k depending only on a
Conclude that Euler’s number, e , is a unique number such that (d)/(dx)((e)^(x))=(e)^(x) , that is, (e)^(x) is its own derivative
Logarithmic functions
Define the logarithm of a number y , where y>0 , to any positive base a as the index to which a is raised to give y
Use the notation log_{a}⁡y for the logarithm of y to the base a
Define the natural logarithm ln⁡a=log_{e}⁡a
Use digital tools to determine rational and irrational values of exponential and logarithmic expressions
Evaluate (4)^((1)/(3)) ,  (e)^(3) and log_{10}⁡5 to two significant figures.
Explain that y=(a)^(x) is equivalent to x=log_{a}⁡y for a>0  and a≠1 , and use the equivalence to solve equations of the form (a)^(x)=b , for a>0
Solve (e)^(x-2)=12 .
Recognise and use the logarithmic properties: log_{a}⁡(a)^(x)=x for all real x , (a)^(log_{a}⁡x)=x where x>0
Solve (e)^(2ln⁡x)-ln⁡((e)^(x))-4=0 .
Derive the laws of logarithms from the laws of indices log_{a}⁡m+log_{a}⁡n=log_{a}⁡(mn) , log_{a}⁡m-log_{a}⁡n=log_{a}⁡((m)/(n)) and log_{a}⁡((m)^(n))=nlog_{a}⁡m
Justify the logarithmic results log_{a}⁡a=1 , log_{a}⁡1=0 and log_{a}⁡((1)/(x))=-log_{a}⁡x
Apply the logarithmic laws and results to simplify expressions, solve equations and prove results, using digital tools where necessary
Solve log_{2}⁡x+log_{2}⁡(x-3)-log_{2}⁡(x+2)=2 .
Prove the change of base rule log_{a}⁡x=(log_{b}⁡x)/(log_{b}⁡a) and use it to solve problems
Graph the logarithmic function y=log_{a}⁡x for a>0 and a≠1
Use graphing applications to identify the graphs of y=(a)^(x) and y=log_{a}⁡x as reflections of each other in the line y=x , in cases where a>1 and 0<a<1

Connections

Course/Stage/Focus area/Post-school paths

The graphs of the exponential functions y=kax and y=ka-x are reflections of each other over the y-axis.

Mathematics Advanced Year 11 Graph transformations

ex is its own derivative.

Mathematics Advanced Year 11 Introduction to differentiation

A logarithm is an index and the logarithmic laws are derived from the index laws.

Mathematics Advanced Year 11 Working with functions

The nth term of a geometric series can be modelled as an exponential function of n.

Mathematics Advanced Year 12 Sequences and series

Financial problems involving compound interest, depreciation, annuities and loans can be modelled and solved using exponentials and logarithms.

Mathematics Stage 5 Financial mathematics B

Mathematics Advanced Year 12 Financial mathematics

The graphs of y=ax and y=loga⁡x are reflections of each other in the line y=x and are inverse functions.

This reflective property can be used when solving integration problems involving logarithms and exponentials.

Mathematics Extension 1 Year 11 Further work with functions

Mathematics Advanced Year 12 Integral calculus

Logarithmic scales are useful to represent a variable that ranges over a large set of values and are used to model and solve problems involving decibels (dB) in acoustics, seismic scales for earthquakes, magnitudes of stars and the pH scale in chemistry.

Logarithmic scales are based on the concept of logarithm, and the process of solving problems involving logarithmic scales involves using exponentials.

Mathematics Stage 5 Logarithms

Mathematics Advanced Year 12 Further graph transformations and modelling

Calculus can be applied to exponential functions and logarithmic functions.

Mathematics Advanced Year 12

  • Differential calculus
  • Integral calculus

The probability density function for the normal distribution is an exponential function base e. 

Mathematics Advanced Year 12 Random variables

The integral of a function of the form ax is a logarithmic function.

Mathematics Advanced Year 12 Integral calculus

Mathematics Extension 1 Year 12 Further calculus skills

Mathematics Extension 2 Year 12 Further integration

Growth and decay situations can be modelled using exponentials. Logistic growth can be modelled by a differential equation and the logistic equation involving the exponential function e-x.

Mathematics Advanced Year 12

  • Sequences and series
  • Applications of calculus

Mathematics Extension 1 Year 12 Further applications of calculus

Results involving logarithmic or exponential expressions can be proven using mathematical induction.

Mathematics Extension 2 Year 12 The nature of proof

Problems involving resisted motion can be solved using logarithms.

Mathematics Extension 2 Year 12 Applications of calculus to mechanics

The surge function, C=ate-bt where a and b are constants, is a model for drug concentration over time and is used in medicine.

The sigmoid function, p=11+e-x, used in data science returns a value between 0 and 1 for any input x.

Content

Exponential functions


  • Graph the exponential functions y=kax and y=ka-x for constants a and k where a>0, a≠1 and k≠0, and identify its asymptote, y-intercept, domain and range



  • Describe the behaviour of y=kax and y=ka-x as x→∞ and x→-∞


    For y=2x, as x→-∞, y→0 and as x→∞, y→∞.

  • Examine the gradient of the tangent to the curve y=ax at its y-intercept for varying values of a, and verify using graphing applications that there is a unique number e ≈ 2.71828182845 ..., such that the gradient of the tangent to y=ex at x=0 is 1, and call this number e Euler’s number



  • Examine the gradient function of y=ax with graphing applications and identify that the gradient function is ddxax=kax, for some constant k depending only on a



  • Conclude that Euler’s number, e, is a unique number such that ddxex=ex, that is, ex is its own derivative



Logarithmic functions


  • Define the logarithm of a number y, where y>0, to any positive base a as the index to which a is raised to give y



  • Use the notation loga⁡y for the logarithm of y to the base a



  • Define the natural logarithm ln⁡a=loge⁡a



  • Use digital tools to determine rational and irrational values of exponential and logarithmic expressions


    Evaluate 413, e3 and log10⁡5 to two significant figures.

  • Explain that y=ax is equivalent to x=loga⁡y for a>0 and a≠1, and use the equivalence to solve equations of the form ax=b, for a>0


    Solve ex-2=12.

  • Recognise and use the logarithmic properties: loga⁡ax=x for all real x, aloga⁡x=x where x>0


    Solve e2ln⁡x-ln⁡ex-4=0.

  • Derive the laws of logarithms from the laws of indices loga⁡m+loga⁡n=loga⁡mn, loga⁡m-loga⁡n=loga⁡mn and loga⁡mn=nloga⁡m



  • Justify the logarithmic results loga⁡a=1, loga⁡1=0 and loga⁡1x=-loga⁡x



  • Apply the logarithmic laws and results to simplify expressions, solve equations and prove results, using digital tools where necessary


    Solve log2⁡x+log2⁡(x-3)-log2⁡x+2=2.

  • Prove the change of base rule loga⁡x=logb⁡xlogb⁡a and use it to solve problems



  • Graph the logarithmic function y=loga⁡x for a>0 and a≠1



  • Use graphing applications to identify the graphs of y=ax and y=loga⁡x as reflections of each other in the line y=x, in cases where a>1 and 0<a<1

Content
Establish using graphing applications that replacing x by -x in the equation of a graph corresponds to the reflection of the graph in the y -axis, and that replacing y by -y   corresponds to a reflection in the x -axis
Establish using graphing applications that replacing x by x-a in the equation of a graph corresponds to a horizontal translation of a graph by a , that replacing y by y-b corresponds to a vertical translation by b , and recognise that the sign of a and b determines the direction of the translation
Describe a horizontal dilation as a stretch from the y -axis and a vertical dilation as a stretch from the x -axis
Establish using graphing applications that replacing x by (x)/(k) in the equation of a graph corresponds to a horizontal dilation of a graph by a factor of k , that replacing y by (y)/(l) corresponds to a vertical dilation by a factor of l , and determine the effects on the graph when the magnitude of the dilation factor lies between 0 and 1
A dilation stretches up and down from the x -axis, or right and left from the y -axis.
Establish, using graphing applications, replacing x by (x)/(k) and replacing y by (y)/(k) in the equation of a graph corresponds to a dilation by a factor of k , that is, an enlargement of the graph when k>1 and a reduction of the graph when 0<k<1
An enlargement enlarges a graph in all directions from the origin.
Apply reflections, translations and dilations to functions within the scope of the Mathematics Advanced course, excluding trigonometric functions, determine the function rule and the graph of the transformed function, the domain and range of the transformed graph, any intercepts, asymptotes and discontinuities where appropriate, and describe which transformations have been applied

Graph circles given their equations and find the equation of a circle from its graph
Recognise that the order in which individual transformations are applied to functions is important

content.name: 📜 Content
content.value:
Connections

Course/Stage/Focus area/Post-school paths

Transformations are related to the concept of commutativity. Any two translations commute. Any two dilations commute. A translation and a dilation commute if one is vertical and the other is horizontal.

Mathematics Stage 4 Algebraic techniques

Reflections and translations are congruence transformations. Enlargements and reductions are similarity transformations.

Mathematics Stage 5

  • Properties of geometrical figures A
  • Properties of geometrical figures B
  • Properties of geometrical figures C

Two reflections, one horizontal and one vertical, in either order, result in a rotation of 180°, and this is the reason for the two minus signs in the algebraic test f-x=-f(x) for oddness.

Mathematics Advanced Year 11 Working with functions

Symmetry properties should be used in sketching functions, including the oddness and evenness of functions.

Mathematics Advanced Year 11 Working with functions

Transformations can be applied to trigonometric functions and transformations of functions can be used to model and solve problems.

Mathematics Advanced Year 12 Further graph transformations and modelling

The probability density function for the standard normal distribution can be transformed to obtain the non-standard normal distribution.

Mathematics Advanced Year 12 Random variables

Transformations can be applied in statistics such that when a constant, c, is added to every item in a distribution, then c is added to the mean but the variance remains unchanged. This is known as the transformation rule in statistics.

Mathematics Advanced Year 12 Random variables

A function is reflected in the line y=x to obtain an inverse relation or function.

Mathematics Extension 1 Year 11 Further work with functions

Mathematics Extension 1 Year 12 Inverse trigonometric functions

The graph of the absolute value function y=x involves a reflection of the line y=x for x<0.

Mathematics Advanced Year 11 Working with functions

Vectors, complex numbers and matrices can be used to represent transformations.

Mathematics Extension 1 Year 12 Introduction to vectors

Mathematics Extension 2

  • Further work with vectors
  • Introduction to complex numbers

Tertiary mathematics

Data transformation functions are used to increase data quality to make accurate predictions in machine learning.

Real-world applications

content.name: 📜 Content
content.value:
• Students could use graphing applications to confirm that reflections in the y-axis and x-axis are respectively horizontal and vertical dilations with factor -1.
  • Students should understand that a dilation or enlargement with a negative factor can be affected by a reflection or 180° rotation, followed by a dilation or enlargement with the opposite factor.
  • The transformation y=-f(-x) rotates the graph 180° about the origin. Students could use a suitable object to show that a reflection in the y-axis and a reflection in the x-axis, in either order, is a rotation of 180° about the origin.
  • Students could find all reflection and rotation symmetries of the circle x2+y2=r2 but this is not essential content.
  • Students could examine how rearrangement of the algebraic representation of a function can change the process of creating its graph. For example, the graph of y=fx + 62 can be rearranged to y=fx2+3 and consequently the same graph can be created using appropriate dilations and translations but in the reverse order.

content.name: 📜 Content
content.value:
Purpose

The study of functions and their transformations is important in developing students’ ability to find connections and patterns, to communicate concisely and precisely, to use algebraic techniques and manipulations, to analyse, model and solve problems, and to predict future outcomes in areas such as finance, economics, data analysis, marketing and weather.

Key terms

  • circle
  • dilation factor
  • discontinuity
  • domain
  • enlargement
  • function
  • horizontal dilation
  • horizontal translation
  • range
  • reduction
  • reflection
  • transformation
  • translation
  • vertical dilation
  • vertical translation

Related Stage 5 Path content

  • Algebraic techniques B
  • Algebraic techniques C
  • Linear relationships C
  • Non-linear relationships C
  • Logarithms
  • Functions and other graphs

Sequencing advice

The content in the focus area Graph transformations builds on content in:

  • Mathematics Advanced Year 11 Working with functions
  • Mathematics Advanced Year 11 Exponential and logarithmic functions.

Making connections

Considerations

Diversity of learners

Outcomes

develops understanding and fluency in mathematics through exploring and connecting mathematical concepts, choosing and applying mathematical techniques to solve problems, and communicating their thinking and reasoning coherently and clearly

Content
Sets and set notation
Define a set as a collection of objects, called the elements of the set, and represent a set using notation such as {2,3,5,7} and {0,2,4,6,…}
Use the notation n(A) or |A| to represent the number of elements in a finite set A
The number of elements in set A={1,3,5} is written as n(A)=3 , or |A|=3 .
Define the empty set as the set with no elements, denoted in set notation as ∅
Use the notation over(A, ¯) , A' or (A)^(c) to represent the complement of a set A with respect to some universal set U
Define A to be a subset of B if all the elements of A are elements of B
Define the intersection A∩B of sets A and B to be the set of elements that are in A and in B
Define the union A∪B of sets A and B to be the set of elements that are in A or in B
Define sets A and B to be disjoint if A∩B=∅ , that is, they have no elements in common
Use Venn diagrams in practical situations to represent and interpret sets that may intersect in various ways within a universal set
Establish and use the rule |A∪B|=|A|+|B|-|A∩B|
Probability
Define an experiment or a trial to be any procedure that can be infinitely repeated and has a well-defined set of possible outcomes known as the sample space, denoted S
Identify an event A as a subset A of the sample space S
Define the probability of each outcome to be (1)/(|S|) when all the outcomes are equally likely and the probability of the event A to be

Conditional probability
Define conditional probability as the probability that an event A occurs given that another event B has already occurred, and use the notation P(A|B)
Examine conditional probability by restricting the sample space and event spaces in a Venn diagram, using a two-way table, a tree diagram and other arrays
The 2 diagrams below represent the same scenario. When calculating the probability of A given B , the sample space is restricted to event B , which has 63 elements. Event A shares 23 elements with event B. P(A|B)=(n(A∩B))/(n(B))=(23)/(63) .
Image long description: In the table, row one includes column headers A , over(A, ¯) and Total; row 2 includes row header B , 23, 40 and 63; row 3 includes row header B , 30, 7 and 37; and row 4 includes row header Total, 53, 47 and 100. Use the formulas for P(A|B) to solve practical problems involving conditional probability
Define two events to be independent if the occurrence of one event does not affect the probability that the other event occurs
Explain that two events A and B are independent means  P(A, B)=P(A) and P(B, A)=P(B) , and show algebraically that if one of these formulas is true, then the other is also true
Use the formula P(A|B)=(P(A∩B))/(P(B)) , and the test P(A, B)=P(A) for independence to prove that if two events are independent, then P(A∩B)=P(A)×P(B) , and to prove conversely that if P(A∩B)=P(A)×P(B) , then A and B are independent
Solve practical problems involving independent events
Data
Define a random variable as a variable whose value is the outcome of a random experiment
Compare discrete random variables with continuous random variables, describe their differences, and give practical examples of each
The number of customers who arrive at the bank between two certain times is a discrete random variable. The time it takes for a bulb to burn out is a continuous random variable.

Purpose

The study of probability provides a powerful and versatile toolset for understanding and navigating uncertainty and informing decisions in a wide range of disciplines.

The collection and statistical analysis of data is of fundamental importance in society. Conclusions drawn from the statistical analysis of data are used to inform decisions made in government, science, business and industry. It is important that students have a broad understanding of how data and statistics are used, as well as how statistics are misused, resulting in the misrepresentation of information.

  • array

  • conditional probability
  • continuous random variable
  • cumulative frequency
  • discrete random variable
  • disjoint sets
  • element

  • independent events
  • intersection

  • multistage events
  • mutually exclusive events
  • outcome

  • random experiment

  • relative frequency

Set notation can be used to express domains and ranges of functions and relations and solutions to inequalities. Real functions are associations between two non-empty sets.Mathematics Advanced Year 11 Working with functions
Probability concepts can be applied in situations involving permutations and combinations, and when working with probability distributions.Mathematics Year 11 Extension 1 Permutations and combinations

Mathematics Year 12 Advanced Random variables

Mathematics Year 12 Extension 1 The binomial distribution and sampling distribution of the mean
Probability distributions show how probabilities are distributed over the values of a random variable.Mathematics Year 12 Advanced Random variables
The area under a probability density function represents the probability of a continuous random variable falling within a particular range.Mathematics Year 12 Advanced Random variables
Cumulative frequency histograms and polygons are related to frequency histograms and cumulative distribution functions. Mathematics Stage 5 Data analysis A

Mathematics Year 12 Advanced Random variables
Probabilities are used to forecast, predict results and evaluate risk in applications such as the weather, medicine, the stock market and insurance.

Probabilities are used when analysing risk for insurance calculations. For example, insurance premiums that are designed for young adult males who have a higher probability of accidents and insurance claims, and insurance premiums affected by the likelihood of natural disasters such as flooding and bushfires.

Probabilities are applied in politics to navigate uncertainty, inform decision-making, strategise campaigns and assess risks.		Real-world applications
The law of total probability is used in situations where it is easier to calculate conditional probabilities rather than find the probability of the event directly, such as finding the probability of a person having a disease using a medical test.Real-world applications

Considerations

  • When calculating probabilities for multistage events students should be able to identify situations and problems involving both replacement and non-replacement.
  • Students should focus on limiting the sample space as the entry point for conditional probability.

Year 11: Probability and data

Outcomes

MAO-WM-01:

develops understanding and fluency in mathematics through exploring and connecting mathematical concepts, choosing and applying mathematical techniques to solve problems, and communicating their thinking and reasoning coherently and clearly

MAV-11-09:

solves problems involving probability in a variety of contexts

MAV-11-10:

displays and analyses datasets using summary statistics and graphical representations

Content

Sets and set notation


  • Define a set as a collection of objects, called the elements of the set, and represent a set using notation such as 2,3,5,7 and {0,2,4,6,…}



  • Use the notation nA or A to represent the number of elements in a finite set A


    The number of elements in set A=1,3,5 is written as nA=3, or A=3.

  • Define the empty set as the set with no elements, denoted in set notation as ∅



  • Use the notation A¯, A' or Ac to represent the complement of a set A with respect to some universal set U



  • Define A to be a subset of B if all the elements of A are elements of B



  • Define the intersection A∩B of sets A and B to be the set of elements that are in A and in B



  • Define the union A∪B of sets A and B to be the set of elements that are in A or in B



  • Define sets A and B to be disjoint if A∩B=∅, that is, they have no elements in common



  • Use Venn diagrams in practical situations to represent and interpret sets that may intersect in various ways within a universal set



  • Establish and use the rule A∪B=A+B-A∩B



Probability


  • Define an experiment or a trial to be any procedure that can be infinitely repeated and has a well-defined set of possible outcomes known as the sample space, denoted S



  • Identify an event A as a subset A of the sample space S



  • Define the probability of each outcome to be 1S when all the outcomes are equally likely and the probability of the event A to be P A = A S



  • Interpret the notation A¯ to be the event ‘A does not occur’, interpret A∩B to be the event ‘A and B both occur’, and interpret A∪B to be the event ‘A or B occurs’



  • Use Venn diagrams to represent the relationship between events within the same sample space, including mutually exclusive events, that is, events that as subsets of the sample space are disjoint



  • Establish and use the rules P A ¯ = 1 - P A and PA∪B=PA+PB-P(A∩B)



  • Use arrays and tree diagrams to determine the outcomes and probabilities for multistage events



Conditional probability


  • Define conditional probability as the probability that an event A occurs given that another event B has already occurred, and use the notation P(AB)



  • Examine conditional probability by restricting the sample space and event spaces in a Venn diagram, using a two-way table, a tree diagram and other arrays


    The 2 diagrams below represent the same scenario. When calculating the probability of A given B, the sample space is restricted to event B, which has 63 elements. Event A shares 23 elements with event B. PA|B=nA∩Bn(B)=2363.

    Image long description: In the table, row one includes column headers A, A¯ and Total; row 2 includes row header B, 23, 40 and 63; row 3 includes row header B, 30, 7 and 37; and row 4 includes row header Total, 53, 47 and 100. In the Venn diagram, the 2 circles are labelled A and B. Circle A contains the number 30, circle B contains the number 40 and the overlapping area contains the number 23. The number 7 sits outside the circles.

  • Establish that PA|B=A∩BB when all outcomes are equally likely by restricting the sample space and event space, and hence PA|B=P(A∩B)P(B), provided B≠0



  • Use the formulas for P(A|B) to solve practical problems involving conditional probability



  • Define two events to be independent if the occurrence of one event does not affect the probability that the other event occurs



  • Explain that two events A and B are independent means PAB=PA and PBA=PB, and show algebraically that if one of these formulas is true, then the other is also true



  • Use the formula PA|B=P(A∩B)P(B), and the test PAB=PA for independence to prove that if two events are independent, then PA∩B=PA×P(B), and to prove conversely that if PA∩B=PA×P(B), then A and B are independent



  • Solve practical problems involving independent events



Data


  • Define a random variable as a variable whose value is the outcome of a random experiment



  • Compare discrete random variables with continuous random variables, describe their differences, and give practical examples of each


    The number of customers who arrive at the bank between two certain times is a discrete random variable. The time it takes for a bulb to burn out is a continuous random variable.

  • Organise finite datasets using a table or a spreadsheet, listing the values, frequency, relative frequency, cumulative frequency, and cumulative relative frequency



  • Graph the frequency, relative frequency, and cumulative frequency histograms and polygons of datasets, using spreadsheets or graphing applications, and identify the mode and median from the graphs, and from tables



  • Use the relative frequency to estimate the probability of results in experiments

Purpose

Sequences are used to model mathematical patterns. In arithmetic sequences the pattern is established by addition and in geometric sequences the pattern is established by multiplication. Series are formed when the terms in a sequence are added together. Sequences and series are useful in the study of limits, convergence and divergence and have applications in fields such as number theory, finance, physics, engineering and statistics.

• Sequences that are neither arithmetic nor geometric could be considered to help students develop an understanding of sequences. For example, what is the nth term of the sequence 1, 4, 9, 16, …?
  • The formula Sn=n2a+an could be developed from examples. The formula Sn=n22a+n-1d can then be developed from Sn=n2a+an.
  • The formula Sn=a(1-rn)1-r can be developed from the identity x-1xn-1+xn-2+…+x2+x+1=xn-1 for whole numbers n≥1. Students can then find a formula for Sn when r=1.
  • The formula Sn=arn-1r-1 is equivalent to Sn=a1-rn1-r which is often used when r>1 .
  • To assist students to understand the concept of the limiting sum of a geometric series, students could use a spreadsheet or a graphing application to plot and list the sequence of partial sums of a geometric series and explore the values of rn or a(1-rn)1-r as n→∞. An example to start with could be the series 12+14+18+ …
  • Summation notation can be used to represent sums of terms of APs, for example
    ∑n=15(2+3n),     and GPs, for example ∑n=143×2n and ∑n=3626-n×10n.

The nth term of an arithmetic sequence can be modelled as a linear function of n. Linear growth or decay problems can be modelled as an arithmetic sequence.

Mathematics Advanced Year 11 Working with functions

The nth term of a geometric sequence can be modelled as an exponential function of n. Exponential growth and decay situations can be modelled as geometric sequences.

Solving sequences and series problems may involve the use of inequalities and logarithms.

  • Working with functions
  • Exponential and logarithmic functions

Summation notation can be used to express results for the expected value and variance of discrete random variables, for the binomial expansion of a+bn, for the sample mean of a sample taken from a population and results to be proved by mathematical induction.

  • Proof by mathematical induction

A recursive formula, or recurrence relation, is a formula that defines each term of a sequence using a preceding term. Its results can be proved by mathematical induction.

Mathematics Extension 2 Year 12 The nature of proof

The Fibonacci sequence is a sequence where each term is the sum of the two preceding terms and has many applications including computer algorithms and biology.

Real-world applications

The representation of numbers in binary form for computer processing is connected to the geometric sequence 1, 2, 4, 8, …

Real-world applications

The large increase in the sum of a geometric series with r≥1 demonstrates why pyramid schemes for making money are not sustainable and why such schemes are illegal in many countries.

Real-world applications

Sequences and series can be used when calculating doubling times, populations, halving times, or the half-lives of radioactive nuclei.

Real-world applications

The functions cos⁡x, sin⁡x and ex can be expressed using a Maclaurin series. ln⁡x can be expressed using a Taylor series.

Year 12: Sequences and series

Outcomes

MAO-WM-01:

develops understanding and fluency in mathematics through exploring and connecting mathematical concepts, choosing and applying mathematical techniques to solve problems, and communicating their thinking and reasoning coherently and clearly

MAV-12-03:

uses arithmetic and geometric sequences and series to model and solve problems

Content

Sequences and series


  • Define a sequence as an ordered list of objects



  • Use the notation an, where n is a positive integer, to represent the nth term of a sequence



  • Distinguish between a finite sequence a1, a2,…, am that terminates at its mth term, for some whole number m≥1, and an infinite sequence a1, a2,… that never terminates



  • Define the nth partial sum Sn of a sequence a1, a2,… to be the sum of the first n terms of the sequence: Sn=a1+a2+…+an, for all whole numbers n≥1



  • Define a series formally as the sum of the terms of an infinite sequence and use the notation a1+a2+a3+… for the series corresponding to the sequence a 1 , a 2 , a 3 …



  • Use summation notation to represent the sum of terms ai to aj of a sequence where j>i, ∑k=ijak=ai+ai+1 +ai+2+ … + aj-1+aj


    ∑k=15(2k+1)=3+5+7+9+11.

Arithmetic sequences and series


  • Define a sequence an to be an arithmetic sequence, or arithmetic progression (AP), if every difference an-an-1 of successive terms is the same where n≥2, that is  an-an-1=d for some constant d called the common difference



  • Develop the formula an=a+(n-1)d for the nth term of an AP, where a is the first term and n≥1, and use it to solve problems



  • Recognise that an is a linear function of n in an AP



  • Develop the formula Sn=n2a+an for the nth partial sum of an AP, and use the formula to solve problems



  • Develop the formula Sn=n22a+n-1d for the nth partial sum of an AP, and use the formula to solve problems



  • Apply the formulas for arithmetic sequences and their partial sums to model and solve growth and decay problems involving a quantity that is a linear function of time



Geometric sequences and series


  • Define a sequence an to be a geometric sequence, or geometric progression (GP), if every ratio anan-1 of successive terms is the same where n≥2, that is an=ran-1 for some non-zero real number r called the common ratio



  • Develop the formula an=arn-1 for the nth term of a GP, where a is the first term and n≥1, and use it to solve problems



  • Recognise that an is an exponential function of n in a GP



  • Prove by expansion x-1xn-1+xn-2+…+x2+x+1=xn-1 for whole numbers n≥1



  • Develop the formula Sn=a(1-rn)1-r for the sum of the first n terms of a GP where r≠1, and use this formula to solve problems



  • Examine the behaviour of an and Sn as n → ∞ for a GP when r<1



  • Develop the formula S ∞ = a 1 - r for the limiting sum of a geometric series with r<1, and use this formula to solve problems



  • Apply the formulas for geometric sequences and series to model and solve growth and decay problems where a quantity is an exponential function of time

Purpose

Calculus involves the study of how things change and provides a framework for developing quantitative models of change and deducing their consequences. It explores the development of analytic and numeric integration techniques and the use of these techniques in solving problems.

The study of calculus is important in developing students’ knowledge, understanding and capacity to operate with and model situations involving change. It also supports students to use algebraic and graphical techniques to describe and solve problems, and to predict future outcomes with relevance to science, engineering, finance, economics and the construction industry.

Key terms

  • chain rule
  • constant
  • derivative
  • differentiation
  • exponential function
  • identity
  • logarithmic function
  • natural logarithm
  • normal
  • product rule
  • quotient rule
  • tangent

Related Stage 5 Path content

  • Linear relationships C
  • Logarithms
  • Functions and other graphs

Connections

Course/Stage/Focus area/Post-school paths

The logarithm laws are used to simplify the process of finding the derivatives of logarithmic functions.

Mathematics Stage 5 Logarithms

Mathematics Advanced Year 11 Exponential and logarithmic functions

Exponential functions and logarithmic functions are used in differentiation.

Mathematics Advanced Year 11 Exponential and logarithmic functions

 

The value of Euler’s number, e, can be derived using the squeeze theorem.

Mathematics Extension 2 Year 12 The nature of proof

Proving the result ddx(ax) requires the identity a=eln⁡a.

Mathematics Advanced Year 11 Exponential and logarithmic functions

 

The identity eln⁡x=x, which is used in proving the formula ddxln⁡x=1x, can be established by considering y=ln⁡x and y=ex as inverse functions.

Mathematics Extension 1 Year 11 Further work with functions

The proof of ddxlogax=1xln⁡a uses the change of base rule.

Mathematics Advanced Year 11 Exponential and logarithmic functions

Trigonometric functions and identities are used in differentiation with trigonometric functions.

Mathematics Advanced Year 11

  • Trigonometry and measure of angles
  • Trigonometric identities and equations

Mathematics Advanced Year 12 Further graph transformations and modelling

The chain rule is used in proving many rules of differentiation.

Mathematics Advanced Year 11 Introduction to differentiation

 

Equations of tangents and normals can be used in solving problems involving differential calculus.

Mathematics Advanced Year 11 Introduction to differentiation

 

The pattern of results for higher derivatives of y=ex, y=ekx, y=sin⁡x and y=cos⁡x can be determined using rules for derivatives of exponential and trigonometric functions.

Mathematics Advanced Year 12 Applications of calculus

 

Differentiation is used in solving problems relating to the motion of a particle moving in a straight line and rates of change.

Differentiation of exponential functions is used in problems involving exponential growth and decay.

Mathematics Advanced Year 12 Applications of calculus

Mathematics Extension 1 Further applications of calculus

Differentiation is used in analysing two-dimensional motion using vectors.

Mathematics Extension 1 Year 12 Introduction to vectors

The derivatives of cosec⁡x, sec⁡x and cot⁡x can be useful in finding integrals.

Mathematics Extension 2 Year 12 Further integration

Differentiation of trigonometric functions is used in solving simple harmonic motion problems.

Mathematics Extension 2 Year 12 Applications of calculus to mechanics

Differential calculus is used to calculate marginal cost and to predict maximum profit.

Real-world applications

content.name: 📜 Content
content.value:
• While differentiating sin⁡x, cos⁡x and tan⁡x is an essential part of the course, the derivatives of cosec⁡x, sec⁡x and cot⁡x do not need to be memorised.
  • Students should recognise that use of radians is fundamental to the calculus of trigonometric functions.
  • Once the key rules of differentiating exponential, logarithmic and trigonometric functions are established, students are encouraged to differentiate functions involving combinations of these functions to encourage fluency in applying the rules of differentiation in different contexts. For example, ddxesin⁡xln⁡x requires students to apply the quotient rule and then the chain rule.
  • Some students may benefit from being extended by exploring the following, however this is not essential content:
    • determining ddx(ax) using differentiation by first principles, i.e. ddxax=limh→0⁡ax+h-axh=limh→0⁡ah-1h×ax,  then using technology to explore this limit and determining that it is a constant
    • considering the values of sin⁡xx, tan⁡xx and cos⁡x as x→0
    • using areas of sectors and triangles in a circle to prove geometrically that limx→0⁡sin⁡xx=1, and hence proving ddxsin⁡x=cos⁡x and ddxcos⁡x=-sin⁡x using the result sin⁡A+B=sin⁡Acos⁡B+cos⁡Asin⁡B.
    • using graphing applications to demonstrate that ddxsin⁡x=cos⁡x using differentiation by first principles, by plotting the graph of y=sin⁡x+a-sin⁡aa and analysing the behaviour of the graph as a→0.
    • considering Euler’s number, e, as the sum of the infinite series 1+11+11×2+11×2×3+…

Connections

Course/Stage/Focus area/Post-school paths

The area under a curve is related to the area of composite shapes.

Mathematics Stage 5 Area and surface area A

When a curve lies below the x-axis, the area between the curve and the x-axis can be found using the absolute value.

Mathematics Advanced Year 11 Working with functions

The reflection property of the graphs of  y=ex and y=ln⁡x can be used in solving integration problems related to exponential or logarithmic functions.

Mathematics Advanced Year 11 Exponential and logarithmic functions

 

The symmetry properties of odd and even functions can be used in simplifying and solving integration problems.

Mathematics Advanced Year 11 Working with functions

Finding the distance travelled over a given time interval from a velocity–time graph is related to the definite integral.

Mathematics Advanced Year 11 Introduction to differentiation

The area under the curve y=1x  between x=1 and x=k is the natural logarithm of a number k>1 in which case e is the value of k for which this area equals 1.

Mathematics Advanced Year 11 Exponential and logarithmic functions

Displacement or distance travelled can be found by integrating a velocity function with respect to time. Velocity can be found by integrating an acceleration function with respect to time.

Mathematics Advanced Year 12 Applications of calculus

Finding the probability of a continuous random variable involves finding the area under a curve.

Mathematics Advanced Year 12 Random variables

The Trapezoidal rule can be used to approximate E(X) and VarX for continuous random variables.

Mathematics Advanced Year 12 Random variables

The volume of a solid of revolution can be found using integration and the Trapezoidal rule can be used to approximate volumes of revolution.

Differential equations can be solved using integration.

Mathematics Extension 1 Year 12 Further applications of calculus

Integration is used in analysing two-dimensional motion using vectors.

Mathematics Extension 1 Year 12 Introduction to vectors

Integration is used in solving simple harmonic motion problems.

Mathematics Extension 2 Year 12 Applications of calculus to mechanics

To calculate the Gini coefficient, which is a measure of the distribution of income across a population, the area under the Lorenz curve needs to be calculated using integration or by approximation.

Real-world applications

Integration is used to find the average value of a function, the length of a curve or the surface area of a solid.

Simpson’s rule uses a quadratic equation through three given points to estimate the area under a curve.

Tertiary mathematics

Integration is used in engineering to determine the geometry of a building. Integration is used in physics to calculate work and the centre of mass.

Real-world applications

Image long description: Two graphs are shown. Figure 1 on the left, shows a curve y=f(x) and marks a and b on the x axis and marks the distance between them as b-a. Two vertical lines are marked: f(a) at a, and f(b)at b. In Figure 2 on the right, the same diagram is drawn as before, but there is also a vertical line in the middle, which splits the trapezium into two trapezia.

  • Students may choose to use a general form of the Trapezoidal rule when there are n sub-intervals such as: ∫abfxdx≈b-a2nfa+fb+2fx1+…+fxn-1 where a=x0 and b=xn, and the values of x0,x1,x2,…,xn are found by dividing the interval a≤x≤b into n equal sub-intervals.
  • When applying the Trapezoidal rule, students are not restricted to applying a formula when setting out their solution. Using tables or simply considering the areas of different trapezia with common width are appropriate methods for approximating definite integrals using the Trapezoidal rule.
  • Some students may benefit from being extended by modelling the function Fx=∫axftdt using graphing applications, and examining the rate of change of the area as x varies, leading to the result F'x=ddx∫axf(t)dt=f(x) but this is not essential content.
  • The approximation of a region’s area by adding up multiple simple shapes is called a Riemann sum.
  • Students could explore different methods of approximating the area under a curve, including using different shapes.
  • Some students may benefit from using graphing applications to explore areas of unbounded regions that have limiting areas in preparation for working with probability density functions, for example: finding that ∫0ae-xdx→1 as a→∞, but that ∫1a1xdx→∞ as a→∞ shows that diagrams sometimes do not pick up huge differences in behaviour. This is not essential content
  • Students may use notations such as ∫-∞0 and ∫0∞ when representing unbounded regions but this is not essential content.

content.value:
• Students should note that for ∫abfxdx the function f(x) must be continuous on the closed interval a≤x≤b, and that it is not possible to integrate across a discontinuity, including discontinuities at the endpoints of the domain.
  • It is appropriate for students to derive general results for integration by reversing the process of differentiation. Alternative derivations are not required in this course.
  • The method of integration by substitution is not required in this course. Students will be expected to establish results such as ∫cos⁡ax+b dx=1asin⁡ax+b+c by differentiating a suitable function. Students should practise the process of integrating f'xfx by inspection, without a formal change of variable. Further techniques of integration are covered in the Mathematics Extension courses.
  • To derive the formula ∫1xdx=ln |x|+C where x≠0 students could:
    Prove by differentiation that for x>0, ∫1xdx=ln⁡x+C, for some constant C, and explain why this formula does not work for x<0.
    Prove by differentiation that for x<0, ∫1xdx=ln⁡(-x)+C, for some constant C, and explain why this formula does not work for x>0.
    Combine the results above to yield the result ∫1xdx=ln⁡x+C, for some constant C, where x≠0, and recognise that no definite integral of 1x can be formed on any closed interval that includes the discontinuity at x=0.
  • If the curve y=fx is approximated on the interval a≤x≤b by the straight line passing through a,fa and b,fb, the area under the curve may be estimated by the area under the line as shown in Figure 1. This approximates ∫abfxdx by the area of a trapezium, which may be calculated using b-a2fa+fb. By dividing the base into two equal sub-intervals (see Figure 2), and using a linear approximation of f(x) on each sub-interval, the area is approximated by two trapeziums. The method extends to dividing the interval into n equal sub-intervals of width h=b-an, and using a ‘trapezoidal approximation’ on each sub-interval.

Purpose

Calculus involves the study of how things change and provides a framework for developing quantitative models of change and deducing their consequences. It explores the development of analytic and numeric integration techniques and the use of these techniques in solving problems.

The study of calculus is important in developing students’ knowledge, understanding and capacity to operate with and model situations involving change. It also supports students to use algebraic and graphical techniques to describe and solve problems, and to predict future outcomes with relevance to science, engineering, finance, economics and the construction industry.

  • identity
